intro: Before you can read a big book, it helps to know what it is. This unit is about the Tanakh, the Hebrew Bible. You will learn its three parts and its twenty-four books. You will see how it is written on a scroll, in Hebrew, from right to left. And you will find out how Jewish communities read it, one piece each week, all year long.

Then you will follow the story of the Torah, its first five books, from the first day of the world to the edge of the land. It is one long journey: a family leaves a city called Ur, moves to Egypt, walks out again with Moses, stops at a mountain and wanders for forty years. Jewish tradition reads the five books as one story held together by a covenant.

By the end of this unit you will be able to name the three parts of the Tanakh and the five books of the Torah in Hebrew and English. You will be able to tell the Torah's story in order, stop by stop. And you will know what a scroll, a scribe, a parashah and a covenant are.
bigQuestion: What is the Tanakh, and what one story do its first five books tell?

timeline.t: The Torah's story opens with the world being made in six days and a rest on the seventh
The Torah says Abram and Sarai leave home for a land they do not know
Joseph's brothers and their father Jacob move the whole family to Egypt
A new Pharaoh makes the children of Israel slaves
The night of Passover; the people leave Egypt in a hurry
At Mount Sinai the Torah says God speaks the Ten Sayings
Leviticus: the holiness laws, including loving your neighbor as yourself
Twelve spies look at the land; the people wander forty years
Moses's last speeches: keep the covenant, choose life
Moses sees the land from Mount Nebo and dies; Joshua takes over
The whole Torah is read aloud, one parashah each Shabbat, and begins again on Simchat Torah

words.d: the Hebrew Bible; a name made from the first letters of Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim
"teaching"; the first five books of the Tanakh, kept as one long scroll
"prophets"; the second part of the Tanakh, with history and the words of the prophets
"writings"; the third part of the Tanakh, with songs, sayings and short books
the language of almost all of the Tanakh, read from right to left
a person trained to write a Torah scroll by hand; in Hebrew, a sofer
"portion"; the section of the Torah read aloud in one week
the fall holiday when the yearly reading of the Torah ends and begins again
"In the beginning"; the Hebrew name of Genesis
a binding agreement; in the Torah, the bond between God and Abraham's family and later the whole people
the tent the people built to carry with them in the wilderness; the tabernacle
"Moses our teacher"; the name Jewish tradition gives Moses

test.q: The name Tanakh is made from the first letters of which three words?
test.why: Tanakh comes from Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim, its three parts in order.

test.q: How many books does Jewish tradition count in the Tanakh?
test.why: The traditional Jewish count is 24: 5 in the Torah, 8 in Nevi'im, 11 in Ketuvim.

test.q: Which of these is true of a Torah scroll?
choices: It is printed by a machine on paper
It has pictures on every page
It is written by hand on parchment with no vowel marks
test.why: A sofer writes the scroll by hand on parchment. The vowel dots are left out.

choices: A pointer used to follow the words on the scroll
The cabinet that holds the scrolls
test.why: Yad means "hand." It is the pointer the reader uses so fingers do not smudge the ink.

test.q: Why do Jewish communities read the Torah in weekly portions?
choices: So the whole Torah is read aloud over one year
Because each portion is a different book
Because the scribe writes one portion a week
test.why: One parashah is read each Shabbat, so the whole Torah is finished in about a year and then begins again.

test.q: In what order does the Christian Old Testament differ from the Tanakh?
choices: It ends with Malachi instead of Chronicles
test.why: The Old Testament holds the same books in a different order. It ends with Malachi; the Tanakh ends with Chronicles.

test.q: Which translation does this course read, and when was it made?
choices: A translation made in Chicago in 2000
test.why: The course reads the JPS translation of 1917, made by a group of Jewish scholars in Philadelphia.

test.q: Which list gives the five books of the Torah in Hebrew, in order?
test.why: The order is Bereshit (Genesis), Shemot (Exodus), Vayikra (Leviticus), Bamidbar (Numbers), Devarim (Deuteronomy).

test.q: What does the Torah say God promised Abraham in the covenant?
choices: A land and a big family
test.why: Genesis says the covenant with Abraham included a land and many descendants. The rainbow belongs to Noah's story.

test.q: Who watched over baby Moses in the basket?
test.why: Exodus says Moses's sister Miriam watched the basket until Pharaoh's daughter found it.

test.q: What do Jewish families eat on Passover to remember leaving Egypt in a hurry?
choices: Matzah, flat bread that did not rise
test.why: The Torah says the bread had no time to rise, so families eat matzah on Passover.

choices: A tent the people carried with them, with the tablets inside
A city built by slaves in Egypt
test.why: The Mishkan, or tabernacle, was a movable tent. Exodus gives every detail of how it was built.

test.q: Which book of the Torah is mostly Moses's speeches?
test.why: Deuteronomy, or Devarim, is Moses speaking to the new generation before they enter the land.

test.q: What happens at the very end of the Torah?
choices: Moses sees the land from Mount Nebo and dies
test.why: Deuteronomy 34 ends the Torah with Moses's death on Mount Nebo. Joshua's crossing is in the next book.

test.q: Why do some readers say the Torah's ending keeps the story open?
choices: Because the last chapter is missing
Because the scroll cannot be rolled back
Because the people are at the edge of the land, not yet inside
test.why: The Torah stops with the people by the Jordan. Some readers say this lets every generation feel it is still on the journey.

write.prompt: Is the Torah one story or five separate books? Use Genesis 12:1–5 (Abram leaves home), Exodus 20:8 (one of the Ten Sayings) and Deuteronomy 34:1–5 (Moses on Mount Nebo). Say what each passage says, and explain how Jewish tradition connects them with the idea of covenant.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse every time you use a passage.
Say "the Torah says" or "Jewish tradition teaches" when you describe a belief.
Use the unit's words: covenant, Bereshit, parashah, Mishkan.
Tell what the passages say and how readers read them; you do not have to say whether they are true.
Keep your sentences short. One idea in each.
